summary.value: This paper introduces TSR-Suite, a dataset covering time series perception, extrapolation and decision-making tasks. This dataset is large in size so that it could support both evaluation and training of time series reasoning models. With the collected training trajectories, the paper introduces TIMEOMNI-1, the first unified reasoning model to tackle time series reasoning tasks. TIMEOMNI-1 achieves superior performance over current landscape of time series reasoning models. Extensive ablation and analysis studies confirms the effectiveness of CoT SFT + RL and multi task joint training paradigm.

strengths.value:
The paper is well-positioned and well-motivated, easy to follow and very clear in structure. 
The paper clearly identifies limitations in current time series benchmarks for time series reasoning and introduces the new dataset with clear goals and well-established data annotation pipeline. 
Though the training paradigm is not novel, the adaptation to time series domain demonstrated great execution. 
Analysis and ablation studies reveal insights that are very useful for the community.

weaknesses.value: The experimental results on time series reasoning is purely performed on the newly proposed dataset. Although there are certain limitations on existing time series reasoning datasets, it would be helpful to see TIMEOMNI-1's performance on some established time series reasoning benchmarks/datasets.

Thank you for your positive and constructive feedback. Below, we provide detailed responses addressing each comment.

> **W1:** It would be helpful to see TIMEOMNI-1's performance on some established time series reasoning benchmarks/datasets.

We sincerely appreciate for raising this important point. To fully address your concern, we conducted additional experiments on **three external time series QA benchmarks (cross 13 tasks, 3,406 samples)**:

- **MTBench** [1] (real-world time series, 4 tasks, 2,380 samples),
- **TimeSeriesExam** [2] (synthetic time series, 5 tasks, 746 samples),
- **CaTS-Bench** [3] (real-world time series, 4 tasks, 280 samples).

All evaluations include **two baselines**:

- **Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct**, which serves as the base model of TimeOmni-1,
- **The original results** reported by each benchmark **for fair comparison**.

All results have been added to the $\underline{\text{Appendix K of Revised Paper}}$. For your convenience, we summarize the results below, where **higher values indicate better performance**.

**MTBench (Real-world dataset)**

|                                     | FinanceQA (7-Day) | WeatherQA (7-Day) | FinanceQA (30-Day) | WeatherQA (14-Day) | AVG      |
| ----- | ----------------- | ----------------- | ------------------ | ------------------ | -------- |
| *Num of Samples*                    | *484*             | *666*             | *523*              | *707*              | *—*      |
| **Base Model**                      | 62.2              | 44.7              | 53.5               | 36.2               | 49.2     |
| **Original Paper Result**  (GPT-4o) | 65.1              | 41.7              | 52.8               | **44.8**           | 51.1     |
| **TimeOmni-1**                      | **72.1**          | **51.4**          | **66.2**           | 42.6               | **58.1** |

**TimeSeriesExam (Synthetic dataset)**

|                                     | Anomaly Detection | Causality Analysis | Noise Understanding | Pattern Recognition | Similarity Analysis | AVG      |
| ------ | ----------------- | ------------------ | ------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------- | -------- |
| *Num of Samples*                    | *108*             | *72*               | *84*                | *362*               | *120*               | *—*      |
| **Base Model**                      | 37.0              | 44.4               | 44.0                | 50.0                | **59.2**            | 46.9     |
| **Original Paper Result** (Phi-3.5) | 28.0              | **52.0**           | 26.0                | 47.0                | 45.0                | 39.6     |
| **TimeOmni-1**                      | **42.6**          | 37.5               | **56.0**            | **56.4**            | 46.7                | **47.8** |

**CaTS-Bench (Real-world dataset)**

|                                                | Caption Retrieval | TimeSeries Retrieval | Amplitude Comparison | Mean Comparison | AVG      |
| ----- | ---------- | ----------- | ------ | ----- | -------- |
| *Num of Samples*                               | *100*             | *100*                | *40*                 | *40*            | *—*      |
| **Base Model**                                 | **69.0**          | **46.0**             | 87.5                 | 57.5            | **65.0** |
| **Original Paper Result** (LLaVA v1.6 Mistral) | 44.0              | 29.0                 | 43.0                 | 35.0            | 37.8     |
| **TimeOmni-1**                                 | 57.0              | 37.0                 | **92.5**             | **67.5**        | 63.5     |

**Findings:** 

**(1) TimeOmni-1 achieves the strongest gains on MTBench.** MTBench is a multimodal time series QA setting where the auxiliary text ($C$) contains task-relevant information (e.g. external events), **matching our TSR-Suite formulation:** $(R, y) \sim p_\theta(R, y \mid X, C) = p_\theta(R \mid X, C), p_\theta(y \mid R, X, C),$ meaning both the reasoning path ($R$) and final answer ($y$) depend on the interaction between the time series input ($X$) and contextual information ($C$). This alignment explains why TimeOmni-1 even surpasses the originally reported GPT-4o performance.

**(2) TimeOmni-1 perform well on TimeSeriesExam and CaTS-Bench.** In these two benchmarks, the text serves mainly as task instructions rather than auxiliary information, so the reasoning relies almost entirely on the time series modality, which is **less aligned with the multimodal reasoning scope defined in TSR-Suite.** 

**Overall, TimeOmni-1’s strong performance across three heterogeneous benchmarks demonstrates that its learned time series reasoning capabilities generalize across domains and tasks.**

[1] *MTBench: A Multimodal Time Series Benchmark for Temporal Reasoning and Question Answering*, 2025.

[2] *TimeSeriesExam: A time series understanding exam*, 2024.

[3] *CaTS-Bench: Can Language Models Describe Numeric Time Series?*, 2025.

> **Q1:** For event aware-forecasting, how is the reward designed since the output should be a variable length sequence.

Thanks for pointing this out. For the sequence-output task (event-aware forecasting), the full reward design is provided in $\underline{\text{Appendix G}}$. In short, we define a **continuous, length-aware reward** based on the exponential decay of the mean absolute error (MAE). It remains meaningful even across variable-length outputs, as it reflects the **average prediction error for each sample.**

Indeed, **Task 3 (event-aware forecasting) contains training instances with variable length** settings. We list the settings below:

| Dataset        | Input length $\rightarrow$ Output length         |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| SFT/RL/ID Test | (72, 12), (96, 24), (48, 24), (72, 24), (96, 12) |
| OOD Test       | (60, 24)                                         |



---


> **Q2:** How do you split in vs out of distribution data? is it based on data domain?  

Many thanks for pointing this out. TSR-Suite constructs out of distribution (OOD) datasets via **domain**, **geographical**, and **building-level distribution shifts**. The full construction details and statistics of all OOD datasets are provided in $\underline{\text{Appendix D.1}}$ and $\underline{\text{Appendix D.2}}$. For convenience, we summarize the key details below.

**Task 1: Scenario Understanding.** OOD is defined by **domain shift**. OOD samples come from Agriculture, Education, and Healthcare domains, which are *different from the training domains*.

**Task 2: Causality Discovery.** All data come from hydrology domain. OOD is defined by **geographical shift**: ID samples come from rivers in *Eastern Germany*, while OOD samples come from *Bavaria*, a different region with distinct hydrological characteristics.

**Task 3: Event-aware Forecasting.** OOD is defined by **domain shift**: ID samples use human mobility time series (*New York City taxi drop-offs with aligned events*), while the OOD test set uses EWELD (*electricity load time series with weather events*), which differs in scale and event–series interactions.

**Task 4: Decision Making.** All data come from CityLearn [1]. OOD is defined by **building-level distribution shift**: the OOD test set uses two buildings whose load profiles *exhibit distinct temporal patterns compared to those in the training set.*

In summary, TSR-Suite constructs OOD testbed via **domain**, **geographical**, and **building-level distribution shifts**, ensuring that the underlying temporal dynamics deviate from the training distribution.

[1] *The citylearn challenge 2022: Overview, results, and lessons learned*, 2023.

> **Q3:** Are different time series domain roughly evenly distributed across task types to prevent certain task types biased towards certain time series application domains?

Many thanks for pointing this out. The time series domains are **not roughly evenly distributed across task types**, and we clarify the data sources for each task in $\underline{\text{Appendix D.1}}$. For your convenience, **we summarize the domains below**:

|           | In distribution (ID) Testbed                                 | Out-of distribution (OOD) Testbed                           |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Task1** | Climate, Traffic, Society, Economy, Energy                   | Agriculture, Education, Healthcare                          |
| **Task2** | Hydrology                                                    | Hydrology                                                   |
| **Task3** | Traffic (*New York City taxi drop-offs with aligned events*) | Energy (*electricity load time series with weather events*) |
| **Task4** | Energy *(battery arbitrage from CityLearn [1])*              | Energy *(battery arbitrage from CityLearn [1])*             |

Achieving a roughly even distribution across task types is challenging, for the reasons below:

**(1) Achieving domain balance across tasks is currently infeasible because many domains do not provide the labels required for all task types.** TSR-Suite is a preliminary effort. Cross-task domain uniformity would require every domain to provide labels suitable for all task types, which is not realistic. For example, 

- **Task 2 (Causality Discovery)** requires pairs of time series with genuine causal relations. In our setting, causality is defined as water measured at an upstream station influencing water measured at downstream stations [2]. Such clear ground-truth causal structures rarely exist in univariate time series data or multivariate time series in other domains.
- **Task 3 (Event-aware Forecasting)** requires time series aligned with high-quality auxiliary context $C$. This includes events that are certain to occur and influence future temporal patterns (e.g. a scheduled Ed Sheeran concert, as shown in $\underline{\text{Table 15 in Appendix L}}$. Such aligned and **high-quality** multimodal data are extremely scarce in other domains.

**(2) This limitation is common in existing benchmarks.** For instance, in Time-MQA [3], the entire classification task relies solely on the Human Activity Recognition domain, while other tasks do not include this domain at all.

**(3) Despite domain imbalance, TimeOmni-1 demonstrates cross-domain and cross-task generalization.** As shown in our additional experiments responding to **W1**, TimeOmni-1 surpasses the base model on several third-party benchmarks **(cross 13 tasks, 3,406 samples)**. This suggests that the model learns time series reasoning capabilities that **transfer across domains and tasks.**

[1] *The citylearn challenge 2022: Overview, results, and lessons learned*, 2023.

[2] *CausalRivers -- Scaling up benchmarking of causal discovery for real-world time-series*, 2025.

[3] *Time-MQA: Time Series Multi-Task Question Answering with Context Enhancement*, 2025.

---

We once again thank you for taking the time to review our paper and for your insightful and constructive comments. We truly appreciate this opportunity to clarify our work and would be grateful for any further feedback.

Best regards,

The Authors

summary.value: The paper introduces a complete framework for time series reasoning that combines a multi task benchmark and a unified training recipe for large language models. The benchmark, called TSR Suite, covers perception, extrapolation, and decision making with four atomic tasks. The dataset contains more than twenty three thousand examples with a carefully curated subset of hierarchical chain of thought traces for supervision. The model, called TIMEOMNI 1, is trained in two stages. First, supervised fine tuning injects time aware priors using a small set of high quality reasoning trajectories. Second, reinforcement learning encourages correct and well structured solutions using task grounded rewards. Discrete tasks are scored by accuracy. Sequence prediction uses an error based reward that maps the mean absolute error into a bounded score and a length counting reward to ensure the model outputs the correct number of steps. Joint training across the four task families is shown to improve transfer. The model reports sizable gains on causality and decision oriented tasks while preserving general reasoning strength on non time series benchmarks.

strengths.value:
1. The paper tackles time series as a reasoning problem and operationalizes this view with a benchmark that spans perception, extrapolation, and decision making. This scope is broader than pure forecasting and motivates models that can explain and decide.

2. In this paper, task design is aligned to evaluation. Multiple choice tasks allow objective grading and sequence prediction uses metric aligned rewards. This makes the reinforcement signal faithful to the intended competence.

3. The training pipeline is relative simple to adopt. A small number of high quality trajectories teaches decomposition. Task rewards then refine the behavior without requiring domain specific architectures. The division of labor between supervised fine tuning and reinforcement learning is clear and effective.

4. In the paper, evidence for cross task transfer is convincing. The model benefits from learning perception and extrapolation before decision tasks. Zero shot improvements on harder tasks suggest that the benchmark composition is synergistic rather than siloed.

5. The model does not only fit a single dataset but shows robustness when the distribution shifts. The paper also checks general reasoning benchmarks to show that specialization does not degrade broader ability.

weaknesses.value:
1. The contributions mix dataset construction, task design, training recipe, and model evaluation without a clear hierarchy. A contribution map that separates what is new in task formulation from what is new in learning would improve the paper.

2. Although the benchmark size is large, the carefully verified chain-of-thought portion is relatively small. The paper would be stronger with an ablation that quantifies how many verified trajectories are needed and how quality trades off with quantity.

3. Several reported gains are sizable, but the paper does not consistently provide confidence intervals or significance tests for both in-domain and out-of-domain settings.

3. In this paper, reward sensitivity is under explored. A sensitivity sweep and a report of failure cases would help others reproduce the effect.

4. The approach still depends on strict output formatting with explicit think and answer tags. This is practical for research but can be brittle in production. The paper does not explore robustness to prompt variations or noisy instructions.

5. Comparisons to adjacent time series agent benchmarks and live decision settings are brief. Positioning against systems that test forward looking planning or interactive tools would help define the boundary of the proposed benchmark.

**Finding.** The narrow intervals across all tasks indicate that our results are consistent and robust.

> **W4:** In this paper, reward sensitivity is under explored. A sensitivity sweep and a report of failure cases would help others reproduce the effect.
>
> **Q2:** What is the effect of the reward design choices? Do different changes alter stability during reinforcement learning? 

Thanks for your constructive comments. We have added a dedicated reward sensitivity analysis in $\underline{\text{Appendix G.1: Reward Sensitivity Analysis}}$. We conduct controlled sensitivity sweeps over the key reward components ($\alpha$, $R_{\text{count}}$, $\lambda$), and evaluate their effects on training stability. All experiments are trained for **1 epoch**, consuming **130 A100 GPU hours**.

For $\alpha$ and $R_{\text{count}}$, which only affect the reward design of Task 3, we report the MAE curves for Task 3 over 1 epoch. For $\lambda$, we evaluate **the proportion of responses with a positive task reward** $\mathcal{R}_{\text{task}}$ across all tasks over 1 epoch.

**Findings.** **(1) Low sensitivity to $\alpha$ and $R_{\text{count}}$**: varying these coefficients leads to only mild changes in MAE curves, indicating that the RL process remains stable across a broad range of settings. **(2) Format reward is essential**: disabling the format component ($\lambda = 0$) causes the model to collapse after 70 steps, with a sharp drop in the positive ratio of task reward $\mathcal{R}_{\text{task}}$.

Overall, the current hyperparameter choices yield the better trade-off between stability and performance.


---


> **W5:** The approach still depends on strict output formatting with explicit think and answer tags. This is practical for research but can be brittle in production. The paper does not explore robustness to prompt variations or noisy instructions.   

Many thanks for pointing this out. We investigate the robustness of TimeOmni-1 to prompt variations. We design three prompt perturbations:

- **Paraphrased Question.** We use ChatGPT to rewrite the original question while keeping the semantic meaning unchanged.
- **Paraphrased System Prompt.** We use ChatGPT to paraphrase the system prompt while keeping the semantic meaning unchanged.
- **w/o System Prompt.** We entirely remove the system prompt to simulate the extreme case.

We have newly added $\underline{\text{Appendix E.3: Model Robustness to Prompt Variations}}$ in the revised paper to address this question. For your convenience, we also provide the experimental results below. ‘–’ denotes the **w/o System Prompt** setting, in which the model no longer produces the explicit $\\langle think \\rangle$ and $\\langle answer \\rangle$ tags; therefore we do not report SR for this condition.

| Prompt Variations | TASK1 ID (ACC/SR) | TASK1 OOD (ACC/SR) | TASK2 ID (ACC/SR) | TASK2 OOD (ACC/SR) | TASK3 ID (MAE/SR) | TASK3 OOD (MAE/SR) | TASK4 ID (ACC/SR) | TASK4 OOD (ACC/SR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Paraphrase Question** | 86.2/97.8 | 85.3/97.5 | 65.8/99.5 | 60.2/98.8 | **13.90**/90.1 | 150.9/81.5 | 47.1/99.8 | 56.1/99.5 |
| **Paraphrase System Prompt** | 88.9/99.5 | 87.4/98.6 | 66.8/99.8 | 62.8/99.5 | 15.28/93.3 | 152.1/84.0 | 43.6/100.0 | 61.9/100.0 |
| **w/o System Prompt** | 86.5/– | 87.1/– | 68.5/– | 63.3/– | 14.29/– | 150.1/– | 40.4/– | **63.0**/– |
| **Original Prompt** | **90.7**/97.5 | **87.7**/98.3 | **69.3**/99.8 | **64.0**/99.8 | 14.30/93.8 | **145.5**/82.3 | **47.9**/100.0 | 58.9/100.0 |

**Findings.** 

**(1) Paraphrasing either the question or the system prompt leads to minimal performance degradation**, indicating that the model does not rely on specific wording or phrasing.

**(2) Surprisingly, even without the system prompt, the model remains highly robust.** Although it no longer outputs the explicit $\\langle think \\rangle$ and $\\langle answer \\rangle$ tags, we adjust the evaluation script to parse the free-form responses and observe that TimeOmni-1 still maintains strong performance, sometimes even outperforming the original prompt. Manual inspection further reveals that the model continues to follow the reasoning template injected during Stage~1 training, suggesting that the temporal prior has been deeply internalized.

**Overall, these results demonstrate that TimeOmni-1 is highly robust to prompt variations and resistant to perturbed instructions.**

summary.value:
This paper introduces TSR-Suite, a comprehensive time series reasoning dataset containing 23K+ QA pairs across four reasoning-critical tasks (scenario understanding, causality discovery, event-aware forecasting, and decision-making), and TIMEOMNI-1, a unified reasoning model trained via a two-stage curriculum (supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning). The work addresses important limitations of existing time series QA datasets by systematically designing tasks that genuinely require reasoning capabilities and ensuring context sufficiency. The hierarchical Chain-of-Thought annotation process is well-designed, and the experimental results demonstrate strong performance improvements over baseline models, particularly in causality discovery (64.0% vs 35.9% with GPT-4.1).

However, the paper has several significant limitations that prevent it from meeting the ICLR acceptance threshold: (1) The model architecture is not clearly described, particularly how time series data is encoded and processed. The paper appears to use text-based serialization of numerical sequences, but this design choice is not explicitly justified or compared with embedding-based approaches. (2) The scalability concerns are not adequately addressed—the dataset appears limited to short sequences and low-dimensional data, with no evidence of handling long sequences (hundreds/thousands of time steps) or high-dimensional multivariate signals (dozens of dimensions). (3) Related work coverage is insufficient, missing important recent work such as ChatTime and ITFormer that directly address time series QA tasks.

strengths.value:
* **Systematic Task Design**: The paper provides a principled approach to formulating reasoning-critical time series tasks through two design principles: requiring genuine reasoning and ensuring context sufficiency. * **High-Quality Dataset Construction**: TSR-Suite represents a substantial contribution with 23K+ curated samples. The hierarchical CoT annotation pipeline (LLM Analyzer → Human Reviewer → LLM Rewriter) is innovative and ensures both quality and scalability in data construction.
* **Comprehensive Evaluation**: The experimental evaluation is thorough, covering both in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization across diverse domains. The joint training experiments demonstrating mutual gains across capabilities provide valuable insights.

weaknesses.value:
### 1. Model Architecture Omission

**Critical Issue**: The paper fails to clearly describe how time series data is processed and encoded into the language model. From the examples (e.g., sequences shown as `[1.2, 3.4, 5.6, ...]`), it appears that numerical time series are simply serialized as text strings and fed directly to the LLM. However, this design choice is never explicitly stated, justified, or compared with alternative approaches.

**Why This Matters**:

- **Reproducibility**: Without clear specification of input encoding, it is difficult to reproduce the results.
- **Novelty Assessment**: It is unclear whether the approach introduces architectural innovations or simply relies on LLM text understanding capabilities.
- **Comparison Baseline**: The choice of text serialization vs. embedding-based approaches (as used in OpenTSLM, ChatTS, etc.) should be explicitly discussed.

**Specific Questions Unanswered**:

- How are long sequences handled? Are they truncated, sampled, or aggregated?
- What is the token budget for time series data vs. context?
- How are multiple time series (Task 2) represented in the input?
- Is there any preprocessing, normalization, or feature extraction?

**Comparison with Related Work**:

- **OpenTSLM** uses explicit architectural components (SoftPrompt or Flamingo-style Perceiver Resampler) for time series encoding.
- **Time-LLM** uses PatchTST-style tokenization with reprogramming layers.
- The current paper should justify why a simpler text-based approach is sufficient or preferred.

### 2. Scalability and Efficiency Concerns

The paper does not address scalability limitations that are critical for practical deployment:

**Sequence Length Limitations**:

- All examples show short sequences (12-24 time steps).
- There is no evidence of handling longer sequences (hundreds or thousands of steps), which are common in real-world applications (e.g., hourly data over years).
- With text serialization, long sequences would consume substantial token budgets and face LLM context window limitations.

**Dimensionality Limitations**:

- The paper focuses on univariate time series (single-dimensional) or at most pairs of sequences.
- Real-world applications often involve multivariate signals (e.g., 12-lead ECG with 12 dimensions, sensor arrays with 50+ channels).
- No discussion of how high-dimensional multivariate time series would be handled.

**Efficiency Concerns**:

- Text serialization of numerical data is token-inefficient compared to learned embeddings.
- For a sequence of length T, text serialization requires ~T tokens (one per value), whereas embedding-based approaches can compress this.
- The computational cost of processing long text sequences through LLMs is quadratic in sequence length.

**Missing Analysis**:

- No ablation studies on sequence length or dimensionality.
- No efficiency/computation cost analysis comparing text-based vs. embedding-based approaches.
- No discussion of context window limitations or how they were handled.

### 3. Dataset Scope Limitations

While TSR-Suite is substantial in sample size (23K+), the scope appears limited:

**Short Sequences**: Examples suggest sequences are typically short (12-24 steps). Real-world time series reasoning often requires much longer histories.

**Low Dimensionality**: Tasks focus on univariate sequences or pairs. High-dimensional multivariate scenarios are not addressed.

**Limited Complexity**: The chosen tasks (scenario understanding, causality discovery) may not fully capture the complexity of reasoning over diverse time series modalities (e.g., sensor fusion, multi-scale temporal patterns).

**Missing Validation**: There is no evidence that the proposed approach would scale to:

- Sequences with 1000+ time steps
- Multivariate signals with 20+ dimensions
- Complex sensor fusion scenarios

### 4. Insufficient Related Work Coverage

Several important recent works on time series QA and reasoning are not adequately discussed:

**Missing Works**:

- **ChatTime** (Ye et al., 2025): "When LLM Meets Time Series: Can LLMs Perform Multi-Step Time Series Reasoning and Inference" - directly addresses time series reasoning with LLMs, including multi-step reasoning capabilities.
- **ITFormer** (and related work): Methods for bridging time series and natural language for multi-task temporal-textual QA should be compared.
- **Time-R1** (Luo et al., 2025): While cited, the comparison could be more detailed, especially regarding reasoning frameworks.

**Why This Matters**:

- These works represent the current state-of-the-art in time series + LLM integration.
- Without proper comparison, it is unclear what novel contributions TIMEOMNI-1 provides beyond existing methods.
- The architectural choices (text-based vs. embedding-based) should be positioned relative to these alternatives.

### 5. Technical Details Omitted

**Missing Information**:

- Input preprocessing pipeline (normalization, scaling, handling of missing values)
- Tokenization strategy for numerical values (precision, formatting)
- How task-specific prompts are constructed
- Details of the reward function design (mentioned but not fully specified in main text)

**(1) Comparative experiments: text-based vs. embedding-based approaches**

TimeOmni-1 adopts a text-based strategy to represent time series inputs. 

For comparison, we implemented an embedding-based approach by **training a time series encoder from scratch** following the ChatTS architecture, which is conceptually aligned with OpenTSLM’s Soft Prompting and Time-LLM’s patch-based encoding. We use the same base model (Qwen2.5-Instruct-14B) with ChatTS to ensure a fair comparison. Results are summarized below.

| Embedding-based | **88.5**/92.9 | **82.4**/97.7 | 40.3/68.7 | 38.7/62.9 | 22.15/75.1 | 162.23/58.4 | 18.2/59.5 | 20.0/51.9 |


**(2) Discussion of using text serialization**

1. **Text-based strategy is a common and widely used approach.** There exist multiple viable strategies for encoding time series, including text-based (Time-R1, Time-MQA), learned embedding-based (ChatTS, OpenTSLM, Time-LLM), and image-based (TimeMaster) representations.
2. **Time series community currently lacks a universally accepted and pretrained time series encoder analogous to ViT [1] in vision domain.** In the absence of such general-purpose encoders, text-based input remains a stable and architecture-agnostic choice. However, designing a dedicated time series embedding module is a part of our future work.
3. **Our experiments show that a simple MLP-based encoder,** similar to those used in ChatTS, OpenTSLM, and Time-LLM, **does not significantly outperform our text serialization method.** More importantly, it noticeably reduces the success rate of producing valid responses, suggesting a negative impact on the base model’s instruction-following ability. A potential reason for the performance gap is the higher data requirement of the embedding-based method. Training a time series encoder from scratch is data-intensive, and our 2.3k CoT-Data might be inadequate.
4. **Encoder-based approaches introduce clear inference-efficiency drawbacks.** Since our Stage-2 training requires extensive sampling, adapt the same architecture with ChatTS significantly increases inference-time overhead, as demonstrated in our efficiency analysis for **W2-part3**.
5. **Current encoder-only methods mainly improve understanding but remain limited in generative reasoning.** Models such as ChatTS, OpenTSLM, and Time-LLM only add a time series encoder, while generation still relies entirely on the LLM’s next-token prediction. An ideally generative solution would require a dedicated decoder capable of reconstructing time series.

Taken together, the text-based strategy is both effective and efficient for the settings considered in this work, where sequence lengths and input dimensionality is modest. Thank you again for raising this point. We have added the corresponding discussion to the revised paper in $\underline{\text{Appendix F.3: Discussion of Tokenizing Time Series into Text Inputs}}$.

- **Precision control.** We introduce a decimal-place reduction algorithm that limits each value to at most two decimal places while preserving the essential temporal information:

\\begin{cases}
\\lfloor x \\rceil,
& \\text{if } \\displaystyle \\frac{\\lvert x - \\lfloor x \\rceil \\rvert}{\\lvert x \\rvert} < 0.01, \\\\[6pt]
\\text{rounded to at most two decimal places for } x,
& \\text{otherwise}.

- **Resolution control**. For example, in Task 2, although the raw time series data is recorded at a 15-minute resolution, we adopt a 12-hour resolution, following the resolutions used in the original paper [1].

We set the maximum input sequence length to 8192 tokens during training, which is more than 8 times the average tokenized length (1106 tokens). This ensures that long sequences do not cause truncation.

**Third, input preprocessing pipeline.** To retain the original data scale, we do not apply normalization. If any training sample contains missing values (e.g., NaN), we remove that sample entirely.

The current text-based serialization strategy is **sufficient and efficient for the tasks considered in this work**, which do not involve “Sequences with 1000+ time steps” and “Multivariate signals with 20+ dimensions”.

However, we fully recognize the potential of embedding-based representations for handling more complex scenarios, and consider this as an important direction for our future research.    As shown in our ablations in $\underline{\text{(Appendix F.3)}}$, the text-based representation outperforms the learned embedding on most tasks. For general reasoning-style problems, feeding numerical data as text remains **effective and feasible**.

- **Compression introduces information loss and unstable normalization.**
  Even state-of-the-art compression techniques [1] do not show performance gains over non-compressed representations. Compression inherently removes information, and it remains unclear whether LLMs consistently interpret heavily normalized or rescaled time series.

> **W2:** The evaluation section and tables mention an "OOD" dataset, but it's not clear how this is constructed or in what sense it is out of distribution. 

Many thanks for pointing this out. TSR-Suite constructs out of distribution (OOD) datasets via **domain**, **geographical**, and **building-level distribution shifts**. The full construction details and statistics of all OOD datasets are provided in $\underline{\text{Appendix D.1}}$ and $\underline{\text{Appendix D.2}}$. For your convenience, we summarize the key details below.

**Task 1: Scenario Understanding.** OOD is defined by **domain shift**. OOD samples come from Agriculture, Education, and Healthcare domains, which are *different from the training domains*.

**Task 2: Causality Discovery.** All data come from hydrology domain. OOD is defined by **geographical shift**: ID samples come from rivers in *Eastern Germany*, while OOD samples come from *Bavaria*, a different region with distinct hydrological characteristics.

**Task 3: Event-aware Forecasting.** OOD is defined by **domain shift**: ID samples use human mobility time series (*New York City taxi drop-offs with aligned events*), while the OOD test set uses EWELD (*electricity load time series with weather events*), which differs in scale and event–series interactions.

**Task 4: Decision Making.** All data come from CityLearn [1]. OOD is defined by **building-level distribution shift**: the OOD test set uses two buildings whose load profiles *exhibit distinct temporal patterns compared to those in the training set.*

In summary, TSR-Suite constructs OOD dataset via **domain**, **geographical**, and **building-level distribution shifts**, ensuring that the underlying temporal dynamics deviate from the training distribution.

[1] *The citylearn challenge 2022: Overview, results, and lessons learned.*, 2023.

> **Q1:** "It remains unclear which tasks genuinely demand reasoning capabilities over time series." I'm not sure what this means. Several recent works (including those you cite like Merrill et al 2024 and Cow et al. 2024) define tasks that require reasoning over time series.

Many thanks for pointing this out. We agree that several recent works include tasks involving reasoning over time series. However, after surveying **19** up-to-date studies, we found **substantial heterogeneity in task formulations, reasoning requirements, and data assumptions**. We conclude that the field still **lacks a clear definition or boundary for what constitutes "time series reasoning tasks".**

This motivates our contribution in TSR-Suite. We systematically formalize reasoning-critical time series tasks by grounding them in three core capabilities: **perception, extrapolation, and decision-making**. When constructing QA pairs, we propose two principles: **ensuring QA requires reasoning and context sufficiency.** Reviewer XR2U and Reviewer 2VxW both highlighted this as a strength:

> Reviewer XR2U: “*Clear Problem Identification: The analysis of limitations in existing datasets (Figure 1) is **well-executed** and **provides strong motivation for the proposed work.***”
>
> Reviewer 2VxW: *“The paper **tackles time series as a reasoning problem** and operationalizes this view with a benchmark that spans perception, extrapolation, and decision making. **This scope is broader** than pure forecasting and **motivates models that can explain and decide**.”*

In summary, although TSR-Suite remains a preliminary effort, we hope it provides the first systematic guideline and useful insights for the design and development of reasoning-critical time series tasks and time series reasoning models.

---

> **Q2:** "Many questions are overly simple and straightforward, where invoking reasoning leads to over-thinking" and "QA-pairs must reward reasoning". Why is it a problem that reasoning doesn't provide an increase in performance? Is this really an issue with the benchmark, or does it say more about the models themselves? **If the models are overthinking** a reasonable, realistic question then **my instinct would be to improve the models**, not find some set of questions where this wasn't the case. 

Thank you for your insightful and constructive comments.

**(1) We fully agree that improving the models is the natural intuition and also the ultimate goal for addressing overthinking.**
We view the development of models that can adaptively decide when to reason and when not to reason as a promising direction, and we include this in our future scope. Similar ideas have already been explored in text and math reasoning [1-2].

**(2) Improving models and improving datasets are not contradictory. Better datasets are prerequisites for better models.**
As shown in our analysis of limitations in existing time series QA datasets $\underline{\text{(Figure.1 and Appendix C)}}$, without reasoning already achieve optimal performance, which means explicit reasoning neither helps nor is required. However, if we aim to build models with stronger reasoning capabilities, **the tasks themselves must require reasoning rather than encourage pseudo or redundant reasoning on overly simple problems**. In this sense, strengthening the benchmark is a necessary step toward meaningful improvements in time series reasoning capabilities.

We sincerely thank all the reviewers for their insightful comments and valuable suggestions, which have greatly helped us improve our paper.

This paper introduces the **Time Series Reasoning Suite (TSR-Suite)**, the first comprehensive time series reasoning suite containing over 23K samples. It formalizes four tasks spanning three core reasoning capabilities: perception, extrapolation, and decision-making. Based on this, we present **TimeOmni-1**, the first generalized reasoning model for time series data. We provide a comprehensive evaluation and **four key findings**, which we hope will serve as the first systematic guideline for the development of time series reasoning models.

The reviewers expressed positive views on our work, describing the proposed TSR-Suite and TimeOmni-1 as **"a substantial contribution"**, with "**well-executed and provides strong motivation**" and **"innovative"**. The writing was noted as **"easy to follow and very clear in structure"**. Our experiments were considered **"reveal insights that are very useful for the community"**, with particular emphasis on the **"evidence for cross task transfer is convincing"**.

The reviewers also provided many insightful comments. We have made every effort to address all the concerns. $\underline{\text{Below is a summary of the major revisions:}}$

- **TimeOmni-1’s performance on third party time series reasoning benchmarks (Reviewer YkbD *&* Reviewer ruC5)**: We conducted additional experiments on **3 external time series QA benchmarks**, covering **13 tasks** and **3,406 samples**. The results demonstrate that TimeOmni-1 has learned time series reasoning capabilities that generalize across domains and tasks. 

  $\text{Newly added} \rightarrow \underline{\text{Appendix K: Additional Evaluation on External Time Series QA Benchmarks}}$
- **Clarification on time series encoding (Reviewer XR2U)**: (1) We clarified that we directly tokenize the time series as text. (2) We have reproduced and evaluated the embedding-based strategy. Under the setting of this work, tokenizing time series as text outperformed retraining a time series encoder in both performance and inference efficiency, with only a slight disadvantage in memory usage. (3) We note that text-based strategy is a common approach, and we do not claim innovation at the time series embedding level.

  $\text{Newly added} \rightarrow \underline{\text{Appendix F.3: Discussion of Tokenizing Time Series}}$
- **Additional reporting on sequence length, token budget, and dimensionality (Reviewer XR2U)**: (1) In TSR-Suite, Task 1 has a maximum input length of 800 time steps, with an average length of 316.3; the average input series length for each task exceeds 48 time steps. (2) The average total token budget (1,106 tokens) is significantly below the input length limit (32,768 tokens) of our base model Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. (3) While we do not claim able to handle “*multivariate signals with 20+ dimensions*,” we have added experiments expanding Task 2 inputs to 5 dimensions.

  $\text{Newly added} \rightarrow \underline{\text{Appendix D.3: Statistics on Sequence Length and Token Budget}}$
- **Expanded comparisons with ChatTime, ITFormer, and OpenTSLM (Reviewer XR2U)**: We provide additional comparisons against these models, analyzing key differences and the positioning of TimeOmni-1.

  $\text{Newly added} \rightarrow \underline{\text{Appendix I: Reinforcement Learning Training Dynamics}}$
- **Reward sensitivity and prompt variation analysis (Reviewer 2VxW)**: (1) We conducted a reward sensitivity analysis by sweeping key reward components ($\alpha$, $R_{\text{count}}$, $\lambda$) and evaluating their impact on training stability, consuming **130 A100 GPU hours**. (2) We designed three types of prompt perturbations (applied to questions and system prompts), showing that TimeOmni-1 is highly robust to prompt variations.

  $\text{Newly added} \rightarrow \underline{\text{Appendix G.1: Reward Sensitivity Analysis}} \text{ and } \underline{\text{Appendix E.3: Model Robustness to Prompt Variations}}$

- **Scaling of Training Dataset (Reviewer 2VxW)**: We conducted extensive scaling experiments not only for **Stage 1 (SFT)** but also for **Stage 2 (RL)**, thereby evaluating both the quantity and the impact of CoT-Data and RL-Data. These experiments consumed **360 A100 GPU hours** in total.

  $\text{Newly added} \rightarrow \underline{\text{Appendix J: Scaling of Training Dataset}}$

**After a full 8 days of experiments, we have added over 200 new experimental results to address the above concerns.** The revisions are highlighted in $\underline{\text{orange.}}$

The reviewers’ valuable suggestions have been extremely helpful in improving our paper. We are happy to answer any further questions.

We look forward to your feedback.
